claim: Neural responses to expected stimuli are frequently found to be attenuated after statistical learning.
source: Neural responses to expected stimuli are frequently found to be attenuated after statistical learning.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding in the abstract, drawing on existing literature.

claim: A reliable attenuation of neural activity for expected compared to unexpected stimuli was observed in the ventral visual stream.
source: We observed a reliable attenuation of neural activity for expected compared to unexpected stimuli in the ventral visual stream.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI study reported in the manuscript.

claim: Sensory attenuation was only apparent when stimuli were attended.
source: Crucially, this sensory attenuation was only apparent when stimuli were attended, and vanished when attention was directed away from the predictable objects.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental manipulation of attention in the study.

claim: Sensory attenuation vanished when attention was directed away from the predictable objects.
source: Crucially, this sensory attenuation was only apparent when stimuli were attended, and vanished when attention was directed away from the predictable objects.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental manipulation of attention in the study.

claim: Extracting statistical regularities from past input to form expectations about the future has been shown to improve behavior.
source: Extracting statistical regularities from past input in the environment to form expectations about the future has been shown to improve behavior in myriad ways (Bertels et al., 2012; Hunt and Aslin, 2001; Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The acquisition of statistical regularities is thought to occur automatically.
source: Indeed, the acquisition of statistical regularities is thought to occur automatically (Turk-Browne et al., 2009) and affects behavior even in the absence of an intention to learn, or an awareness of, the regularities (Fiser and Aslin, 2002; Brady and Oliva, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Statistical regularities affect behavior even in the absence of an intention to learn or an awareness of the regularities.
source: Indeed, the acquisition of statistical regularities is thought to occur automatically (Turk-Browne et al., 2009) and affects behavior even in the absence of an intention to learn, or an awareness of, the regularities (Fiser and Aslin, 2002; Brady and Oliva, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Many studies documented attenuated neural responses for expected compared to unexpected object stimuli in ventral visual regions in terms of single unit spiking activity in monkeys.
source: Many studies documented attenuated neural responses for expected compared to unexpected object stimuli in ventral visual regions subserving object recognition, both in terms of single unit spiking activity in monkeys (Meyer and Olson, 2011; Kaposvari et al., 2018) and in terms of non-invasively measured BOLD activity in humans (den Ouden et al., 2010; Egner et al., 2010; Richter et al., 2018; for a review see de Lange et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Many studies documented attenuated neural responses for expected compared to unexpected object stimuli in ventral visual regions in terms of non-invasively measured BOLD activity in humans.
source: Many studies documented attenuated neural responses for expected compared to unexpected object stimuli in ventral visual regions subserving object recognition, both in terms of single unit spiking activity in monkeys (Meyer and Olson, 2011; Kaposvari et al., 2018) and in terms of non-invasively measured BOLD activity in humans (den Ouden et al., 2010; Egner et al., 2010; Richter et al., 2018; for a review see de Lange et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Expectation suppression was robustly present when participants attended the objects in V1.
source: In all three regions, expectation suppression was robustly present when participants attended the objects (V1: t(33) = 3.573, p=0.001, dz = 0.613; LOC: t(33) = 3.860, p=5.0e-4, dz = 0.662; TOFC: t(33) = 5.133, p=1.2e-5, dz = 0.880)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI study with statistical support.

claim: Expectation suppression was robustly present when participants attended the objects in LOC.
source: In all three regions, expectation suppression was robustly present when participants attended the objects (V1: t(33) = 3.573, p=0.001, dz = 0.613; LOC: t(33) = 3.860, p=5.0e-4, dz = 0.662; TOFC: t(33) = 5.133, p=1.2e-5, dz = 0.880)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI study with statistical support.

evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI study with statistical support.

claim: Expectation suppression was absent when participants attended the characters at fixation in V1.
source: but absent when participants attended the characters at fixation; that is, when the predictable objects were unattended (V1: t(33) = −0.216, p=0.830, dz = −0.037; LOC: t(33) = −0.831, p=0.412, dz = −0.143; TOFC: t(33) = 0.072, p=0.943, dz = 0.012).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI study with statistical support.

claim: Expectation suppression was absent when participants attended the characters at fixation in LOC.
source: but absent when participants attended the characters at fixation; that is, when the predictable objects were unattended (V1: t(33) = −0.216, p=0.830, dz = −0.037; LOC: t(33) = −0.831, p=0.412, dz = −0.143; TOFC: t(33) = 0.072, p=0.943, dz = 0.012).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI study with statistical support.

claim: Expectation suppression was absent when participants attended the characters at fixation in TOFC.
source: but absent when participants attended the characters at fixation; that is, when the predictable objects were unattended (V1: t(33) = −0.216, p=0.830, dz = −0.037; LOC: t(33) = −0.831, p=0.412, dz = −0.143; TOFC: t(33) = 0.072, p=0.943, dz = 0.012).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI study with statistical support.

claim: Bayesian analyses showed moderate support for the null hypothesis of no expectation suppression in V1 during the character categorization task.
source: Indeed, Bayesian analyses showed moderate support for the null hypothesis (BF10 <1/3) of no expectation suppression in all three regions during the character categorization task (V1: BF10 = 0.188; LOC: BF10 = 0.253; TOFC: BF10 = 0.184).
evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian statistical analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: Bayesian analyses showed moderate support for the null hypothesis of no expectation suppression in LOC during the character categorization task.
source: Indeed, Bayesian analyses showed moderate support for the null hypothesis (BF10 <1/3) of no expectation suppression in all three regions during the character categorization task (V1: BF10 = 0.188; LOC: BF10 = 0.253; TOFC: BF10 = 0.184).
evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian statistical analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: Bayesian analyses showed moderate support for the null hypothesis of no expectation suppression in TOFC during the character categorization task.
source: Indeed, Bayesian analyses showed moderate support for the null hypothesis (BF10 <1/3) of no expectation suppression in all three regions during the character categorization task (V1: BF10 = 0.188; LOC: BF10 = 0.253; TOFC: BF10 = 0.184).
evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian statistical analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: There was a significant interaction between expectation and attention in V1.
source: The robustness of this distinct pattern of expectation suppression for the two conditions was statistically confirmed by an interaction analysis (expectation by attention interaction, V1:, F(1,33) = 7.706, p=0.009, η²=0.189; LOC: F(1,33) = 12.580, p=0.001, η²=0.276; TOFC: F(1,33) = 16.955, p=2.4e-4, η²=0.339).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: There was a significant interaction between expectation and attention in LOC.
source: The robustness of this distinct pattern of expectation suppression for the two conditions was statistically confirmed by an interaction analysis (expectation by attention interaction, V1:, F(1,33) = 7.706, p=0.009, η²=0.189; LOC: F(1,33) = 12.580, p=0.001, η²=0.276; TOFC: F(1,33) = 16.955, p=2.4e-4, η²=0.339).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: There was a significant interaction between expectation and attention in TOFC.

evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: Expectation suppression in LOC was significantly larger for stimulus-driven than non-stimulus-driven voxels.
source: Whereas there was clear evidence for a larger expectation suppression effect in stimulus-driven than not stimulus-driven voxels in higher visual areas (LOC: t(33) = 3.991, p=3.4e-4, dz = 0.684; TOFC: t(33) = 4.654, p=5.1e-5, dz = 0.798)
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus specificity analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: Expectation suppression in TOFC was significantly larger for stimulus-driven than non-stimulus-driven voxels.
source: Whereas there was clear evidence for a larger expectation suppression effect in stimulus-driven than not stimulus-driven voxels in higher visual areas (LOC: t(33) = 3.991, p=3.4e-4, dz = 0.684; TOFC: t(33) = 4.654, p=5.1e-5, dz = 0.798)
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus specificity analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: Suppression was not significantly different between stimulus-driven and not stimulus-driven voxels in V1.
source: suppression was not significantly different between stimulus-driven and not stimulus-driven voxels in V1 (t(33) = −1.057, p=0.298, dz = −0.181).
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus specificity analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: A Bayesian analysis indicated moderate support for the absence of a difference between stimulus-driven and not stimulus-driven voxels in V1.
source: Indeed, a Bayesian analysis indicated moderate support for the absence of a difference between stimulus-driven and not stimulus-driven voxels in V1 (BF10 = 0.307).
evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian statistical analysis of the fMRI data.

claim: There was a larger pupil diameter for unexpected compared to expected trailing images during the objects attended task.
source: There was indeed a larger pupil diameter for unexpected compared to expected trailing images during the objects attended task (Figure 3, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the pupillometry analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The difference in pupil diameter between unexpected and expected images emerged gradually starting ~600 ms after the onset of the trailing object image.
source: This difference emerged gradually starting ~600 ms after the onset of the trailing object image, and was significant between 1.5–2.8 s, as assessed with a cluster permutation test (pcluster = 0.017).
evidence: This is a finding from the pupillometry analysis with statistical support.

claim: The difference in pupil diameter between unexpected and expected images was significant between 1.5–2.8 s.
source: This difference emerged gradually starting ~600 ms after the onset of the trailing object image, and was significant between 1.5–2.8 s, as assessed with a cluster permutation test (pcluster = 0.017).
evidence: This is a finding from the pupillometry analysis with statistical support.

claim: When objects were unattended, no significant difference in pupil diameter was found between the expectation conditions.
source: When objects were unattended, no significant difference in pupil diameter was found between the expectation conditions, and in fact, no timepoint surpassed the cluster formation threshold (i.e., all timepoints p>0.05 uncorrected; Figure 3, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the pupillometry analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The expectation induced difference in pupil diameter was not reliably different between attended and unattended stimuli.
source: However, the expectation induced difference in pupil diameter was not reliably different between attended and unattended stimuli (pcluster = 0.393).
evidence: This is a finding from the pupillometry analysis with statistical support.

claim: When objects were attended, expectation suppression in V1 was more pronounced for trailing images that also resulted in larger pupil dilation differences.
source: Results, displayed in Figure 4A, suggest that, when objects were attended, expectation suppression in V1 was more pronounced for trailing images that also resulted in larger pupil dilation differences (t(31) = 2.464, p=0.019, dz = 0.436).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between pupil dilation and expectation suppression, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The association between pupil dilation differences and expectation suppression was not reliable in LOC when objects were attended.
source: This association was not reliable in LOC (t(31) = 1.413, p=0.167, dz = 0.250; BF10 = 0.466) or TOFC (t(31) = 1.401, p=0.171, dz = 0.248; BF10 = 0.458).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between pupil dilation and expectation suppression.

claim: The association between pupil dilation differences and expectation suppression was not reliable in TOFC when objects were attended.
source: This association was not reliable in LOC (t(31) = 1.413, p=0.167, dz = 0.250; BF10 = 0.466) or TOFC (t(31) = 1.401, p=0.171, dz = 0.248; BF10 = 0.458).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between pupil dilation and expectation suppression.

claim: There was no correlation of pupil dilation differences and expectation suppression when stimuli were unattended in V1.
source: There was no correlation of pupil dilation differences and expectation suppression when stimuli were unattended in any of the ROIs (V1: t(31) = −0.159, p=0.875, dz = −0.028; BF10 = 0.191; LOC: t(31) = −0.125, p=0.901, dz = −0.022; BF10 = 0.190; TOFC: t(31) = 0.177, p=0.861, dz = 0.031; BF10 = 0.192).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between pupil dilation and expectation suppression.

claim: There was no correlation of pupil dilation differences and expectation suppression when stimuli were unattended in LOC.
source: There was no correlation of pupil dilation differences and expectation suppression when stimuli were unattended in any of the ROIs (V1: t(31) = −0.159, p=0.875, dz = −0.028; BF10 = 0.191; LOC: t(31) = −0.125, p=0.901, dz = −0.022; BF10 = 0.190; TOFC: t(31) = 0.177, p=0.861, dz = 0.031; BF10 = 0.192).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between pupil dilation and expectation suppression.

claim: There was no correlation of pupil dilation differences and expectation suppression when stimuli were unattended in TOFC.
source: There was no correlation of pupil dilation differences and expectation suppression when stimuli were unattended in any of the ROIs (V1: t(31) = −0.159, p=0.875, dz = −0.028; BF10 = 0.191; LOC: t(31) = −0.125, p=0.901, dz = −0.022; BF10 = 0.190; TOFC: t(31) = 0.177, p=0.861, dz = 0.031; BF10 = 0.192).

claim: During the object categorization task, participants were more accurate for expected compared to unexpected trailing object stimuli.
source: During the object categorization task, participants were more accurate (W = 457, p=3.2e-4, rB = 0.536) and faster (W = 9, p=3.8e-9, rB = −0.970) for expected compared to unexpected trailing object stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis during the fMRI task.

claim: During the object categorization task, participants were faster for expected compared to unexpected trailing object stimuli.
source: During the object categorization task, participants were more accurate (W = 457, p=3.2e-4, rB = 0.536) and faster (W = 9, p=3.8e-9, rB = −0.970) for expected compared to unexpected trailing object stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis during the fMRI task.

claim: During the character categorization task, no behavioral benefit was observed in terms of accuracy.
source: Conversely, during the character categorization task, no such benefit was observed in terms of accuracy (t(33) = 1.600, p=0.119, dz = 0.274; BF10 = 0.582) or RT (W = 252, p=0.447, rB = −0.153; BF10 = 0.273).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis during the fMRI task.

claim: During the character categorization task, no behavioral benefit was observed in terms of RT.
source: Conversely, during the character categorization task, no such benefit was observed in terms of accuracy (t(33) = 1.600, p=0.119, dz = 0.274; BF10 = 0.582) or RT (W = 252, p=0.447, rB = −0.153; BF10 = 0.273).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis during the fMRI task.

claim: When the predictable objects were attended, behaviorally observed expectation RT benefits and neurally observed expectation suppression were associated in V1.
source: Results, illustrated in Figure 4B, show that when the predictable objects were attended, behaviorally observed expectation RT benefits and neurally observed expectation suppression were associated in both, V1 (t(33) = 2.442, p=0.020, dz = 0.419) and TOFC (t(33) = 2.236, p=0.032, dz = 0.384)
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between behavioral and neural measures, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: When the predictable objects were attended, behaviorally observed expectation RT benefits and neurally observed expectation suppression were associated in TOFC.
source: Results, illustrated in Figure 4B, show that when the predictable objects were attended, behaviorally observed expectation RT benefits and neurally observed expectation suppression were associated in both, V1 (t(33) = 2.442, p=0.020, dz = 0.419) and TOFC (t(33) = 2.236, p=0.032, dz = 0.384)
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between behavioral and neural measures, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: No reliable correlation was found between RT benefits and expectation suppression in LOC when objects were attended.
source: but no reliable correlation was found in LOC (t(33) = 1.384, p=0.176, dz = 0.237, BF10 = 0.439).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between behavioral and neural measures.

claim: There was no association between RT benefits and expectation suppression in any ROI when objects were unattended.
source: There was no association in any ROI when objects were unattended (V1: t(33) = −0.418, p=0.679, dz = −0.072, BF10 = 0.199; LOC: t(33) = −0.374, p=0.711, dz = −0.064, BF10 = 0.196; TOFC: t(33) = 0.179, p=0.859, dz = 0.031, BF10 = 0.186).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between behavioral and neural measures.

claim: Participants indicated the correct trailing image with above chance accuracy for the set of object pairs that was previously attended.
source: Participants indicated the correct trailing image with above chance accuracy for both, the set of object pairs that was previously attended (Figure 5B; performance = 62.1 ± 1.8%, mean ± SE; t(33) = 6.803, p=4.6e-8, dz = 1.167)
evidence: This is a finding from the post-scanning pair recognition task, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Participants indicated the correct trailing image with above chance accuracy for the set of object pairs that was previously unattended.
source: and the set that was previously unattended (performance = 58.7 ± 2.2%; t(33) = 3.905, p=2.2e-4, dz = 0.670).
evidence: This is a finding from the post-scanning pair recognition task.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in accuracy on the pair recognition task between the sets of objects that were previously attended and unattended.
source: There was no statistically significant difference in accuracy on the pair recognition task between these sets of objects (W = 365, p=0.256, rB = 0.227; BF10 = 0.737).
evidence: This is a finding from the post-scanning pair recognition task.

claim: Reaction times were similar for both sets of objects in the pair recognition task.
source: Reaction times were also similar for both sets of objects (objects previously attended: RT = 458.8 ± 25.4 ms; objects previously unattended: RT = 466.5 ± 25.9 ms; t(33) = −1.208, p=0.236, dz = −0.207; BF10 = 0.358).
evidence: This is a finding from the post-scanning pair recognition task.

claim: Object identity could be decoded above chance in V1 when objects were attended.
source: One-sample t-tests or Wilcoxon signed rank test (as applicable) showed that in each of the three ROIs (V1, LOC, TOFC) and tasks (objects attended, objects unattended) object identity could be decoded above chance (V1 attended: 81.1%; W = 595, p=3.3e-7, rB = 1; V1 unattended: 84.8%; W = 595, p=3.2e-7, rB = 1; LOC attended: 37.3%; t(33) = 6.303, p=4.0e-7, dz = 1.08; LOC unattended: 38.0%; W = 583, p=9.7e-7, rB = 0.96; TOFC unattended: 25.0%; W = 476, p=0.002, rB = 0.60)
evidence: This is a finding from the multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA).

source: One-sample t-tests or Wilcoxon signed rank test (as applicable) showed that in each of the three ROIs (V1, LOC, TOFC) and tasks (objects attended, objects unattended) object identity could be decoded above chance (V1 attended: 81.1%; W = 595, p=3.3e-7, rB = 1; V1 unattended: 84.8%; W = 595, p=3.2e-7, rB = 1; LOC attended: 37.3%; t(33) = 6.303, p=4.0e-7, dz = 1.08; LOC unattended: 38.0%; W = 583, p=9.7e-7, rB = 0.96; TOFC unattended: 25.0%; W = 476, p=0.002, rB = 0.60)

claim: Object identity could not be decoded above chance in TOFC when objects were attended.
source: except in TOFC in the attended condition (TOFC attended: 19.6%; W = 383, p=0.143, rB = 0.287; BF10 = 0.388).
evidence: This is a finding from the multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA).

claim: Decoding accuracy was not different between the objects attended and unattended conditions in V1.
source: Moreover, decoding accuracy was not different between the objects attended and unattended conditions in any of the ROIs (V1: t(33) = −1.197, p=0.240, dz = −0.205, BF10 = 0.354; LOC: t(33) = −0.214, p=0.832, dz = −0.037, BF10 = 0.188; TOFC: t(33) = −1.726, p=0.094, dz = −0.296, BF10 = 0.697).

claim: Decoding accuracy was not different between the objects attended and unattended conditions in LOC.
source: Moreover, decoding accuracy was not different between the objects attended and unattended conditions in any of the ROIs (V1: t(33) = −1.197, p=0.240, dz = −0.205, BF10 = 0.354; LOC: t(33) = −0.214, p=0.832, dz = −0.037, BF10 = 0.188; TOFC: t(33) = −1.726, p=0.094, dz = −0.296, BF10 = 0.697).

claim: Attention seems to gate the integration of prior knowledge and sensory input.
source: In sum, our results suggest that visual statistical learning results in attenuated sensory processing for predicted input, but only when this input is attentively processed. Thus, attention seems to gate the integration of prior knowledge and sensory input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings of the study.

claim: The results place important constraints on neurocomputational theories that cast perceptual inference as a process of automatic integration of prior and sensory information.
source: This places important constraints on neurocomputational theories that cast perceptual inference as a process of automatic integration of prior and sensory information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the study's findings.

claim: Expectation suppression throughout the ventral visual stream was observed when objects were attended.
source: The upper row in Figure 2A shows extensive clusters of expectation suppression throughout the ventral visual stream when objects were attended
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: No difference in neural activity was found when the objects were unattended in the whole-brain analysis.
source: but no difference when the objects were unattended (middle row), leading to a significant interaction (bottom row).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Outside the ventral visual stream, additional clusters of expectation suppression are evident in anterior insula and the frontal operculum, the precentral and inferior frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus and supplementary motor cortex, superior parietal lobule, as well as parts of the cerebellum.
source: Outside the ventral visual stream, additional clusters of expectation suppression are evident in anterior insula and the frontal operculum, the precentral and inferior frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus and supplementary motor cortex, superior parietal lobule, as well as parts of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: All non-sensory clusters showed reduced activity for expected objects only when the object stimuli were attended and categorized.
source: Again, all these non-sensory clusters showed reduced activity for expected objects only when the object stimuli were attended and categorized.
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: There was no significant modulation of activity by expectation anywhere in the whole brain analysis when the objects were unattended.
source: There was no significant modulation of activity by expectation anywhere in the whole brain analysis when the objects were unattended.
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: Expected object stimuli were categorized more quickly during the object categorization task.
source: During the object categorization task, the ability to form expectations about the trailing object stimulus was helpful for the participants, and indeed expected object stimuli were categorized more quickly and accurately (see Figure 5A and Expectations facilitate object classification).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Expected object stimuli were categorized more accurately during the object categorization task.
source: During the object categorization task, the ability to form expectations about the trailing object stimulus was helpful for the participants, and indeed expected object stimuli were categorized more quickly and accurately (see Figure 5A and Expectations facilitate object classification).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Significant, bilateral clusters of expectation suppression were evident throughout most of the ventral visual stream in the conjunction analysis.
source: Figure 2B shows the whole-brain results of this conjunction analysis. Significant, bilateral clusters of expectation suppression were evident throughout most of the ventral visual stream.
evidence: This is a finding from the conjunction analysis, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: None of the non-sensory clusters showed significant expectation suppression during both experiments in the conjunction analysis.
source: However, none of the non-sensory clusters showed significant expectation suppression during both experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the conjunction analysis.

claim: Only in the ventral visual stream was there strong and robust evidence for expectation suppression, regardless of whether the predictable relationship was task-relevant or task-irrelevant, as long as the predictable object pairs were attended.
source: Thus, only in the ventral visual stream we found strong and robust evidence for expectation suppression, regardless of whether the predictable relationship was task-relevant or task-irrelevant, as long as the predictable object pairs were attended.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conjunction analysis findings.

claim: All sub-populations in all three ROIs showed significant expectation suppression.
source: Of note, all sub-populations in all three ROIs showed significant expectation suppression (all p<0.05)
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus specificity analysis.

claim: There is a general suppression of activity for expected stimuli in visual cortex, irrespective of whether the visual cortical area is driven by the stimuli.
source: suggesting that there is a general suppression of activity for expected stimuli in visual cortex, irrespective of whether the visual cortical area is driven by the stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the stimulus specificity analysis findings.

claim: In later visual cortical areas (LOC and TOFC) there was significantly more expectation suppression in neuronal subpopulations that were driven by the stimulus.
source: However, in later visual cortical areas (LOC and TOFC) there was significantly more expectation suppression in neuronal subpopulations that were driven by the stimulus, implying a more selective suppression mechanism in these areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the stimulus specificity analysis findings.

claim: Pupil responses have been linked with changes in arousal.
source: Pupil responses have been with linked with changes in arousal (Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pupil dilation scales with surprise.
source: Moreover, pupil dilation scales with surprise (Damsma and van Rijn, 2017; Kloosterman et al., 2015; Preuschoff et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The objects attended and objects unattended tasks showed very similar response accuracies.
source: Overall, the objects attended (classify electronic items) and objects unattended task (classify characters at fixation) showed very similar response accuracies (attended: 94.3 ± 5.4% vs. unattended: 94.0 ± 6.6%, mean ± SD)
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis during the fMRI task.

claim: The objects attended and objects unattended tasks showed only minor differences in RTs.
source: and only minor differences in RTs (attended: 574 ± 150 ms vs. unattended: 602 ± 131 ms, mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis during the fMRI task.

claim: Both tasks were of approximately equal difficulty.
source: This supports the notion that both tasks were of approximately equal difficulty.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral performance data.

claim: The target sample size was n = 34.
source: Our target sample size was n = 34.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the study design.

claim: This sample size was chosen to ensure 80% power for detecting at least a medium effect size (Cohen's d ≥ 0.5) with a two-sided paired t-test at an alpha level of 0.05.
source: This sample size was chosen to ensure 80% power for detecting at least a medium effect size (Cohen's d ≥ 0.5) with a two-sided paired t-test at an alpha level of 0.05.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the study design.

claim: In total, 38 healthy, right-handed participants were recruited from the Radboud University research participation system.
source: In total, 38 healthy, right-handed participants were recruited from the Radboud University research participation system.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant recruitment.

claim: Four participants were excluded, resulting in the desired sample size of n = 34 participants for data analysis.
source: We excluded four participants, following our exclusion criteria (see preregistration document and Data Exclusion) resulting in the desired sample size of n = 34 participants (25 females, age 24.9 ± 4.8 years, mean ± SD) for data analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data exclusion.

claim: Of the four exclusions, three exhibited excessive motion during scanning.
source: Of these four exclusions, three exhibited excessive motion during scanning, and one was caused by the participant falling asleep, thus resulting in an incomplete data set.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data exclusion.

claim: One exclusion was caused by the participant falling asleep, thus resulting in an incomplete data set.
source: Of these four exclusions, three exhibited excessive motion during scanning, and one was caused by the participant falling asleep, thus resulting in an incomplete data set.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data exclusion.

claim: The present study was preregistered at Open Science Framework (OSF) before any data were acquired.
source: The present study was preregistered at Open Science Framework (OSF) before any data were acquired.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about study preregistration.

claim: Increased pupil dilations were associated with larger BOLD responses regardless of whether stimuli were attended and expected.
source: Increased pupil dilations were associated with larger BOLD responses regardless of whether stimuli were attended and expected (attended expected: t(31) = 3.006, p=0.005, dz = 0.531; attended unexpected: t(31) = 4.392, p=1.2e-4, dz = 0.776; unattended expected: t(31) = 5.228, p=1.1e-5, dz = 0.924; unattended unexpected: W = 452, p=2.1e-4, rB = 0.712).
evidence: This is a finding from the supplemental analysis linking pupil dilation and BOLD responses.

claim: Pupil dilation led to slightly stronger BOLD increases when objects were unattended than attended.
source: Pupil dilation led to slightly stronger BOLD increases when objects were unattended than attended (F(1,31) = 5.563, p=0.025, η²=0.152)
evidence: This is a finding from the supplemental analysis linking pupil dilation and BOLD responses.

claim: Pupil dilation had a positive effect on overall BOLD responses in V1.
source: Thus, pupil dilation had a positive effect on overall BOLD responses in V1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the supplemental analysis findings.

claim: The association between BOLD responses and pupil dilation was somewhat larger in non-stimulus-driven than stimulus-driven voxels.
source: Interestingly, this association was somewhat larger in non-stimulus-driven than stimulus-driven voxels (F(1,31) = 9.267, p=0.005, η²=0.230)
evidence: This is a finding from the supplemental analysis of stimulus-driven vs. non-stimulus-driven voxels.

claim: The association between BOLD and pupil dilation is particularly strong for those neural populations that are not driven by the object stimuli.
source: suggesting that the association between BOLD and pupil dilation is particularly strong for those neural populations that are not driven by our object stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the supplemental analysis findings.

claim: There was no difference in baseline pupil size before attended compared to unattended stimuli.
source: Results showed that there was no difference in baseline pupil size before attended compared to unattended stimuli (F(1,31) = 5.226, p=0.484, η²=0.016, BFinclusion = 0.254)
evidence: This is a finding from the supplemental analysis of baseline pupil size.

claim: There was no difference in baseline pupil size before expected compared to unexpected stimuli.
source: nor before expected compared to unexpected stimuli (F(1,31) = 0.001, p=0.926, η²=2.8e-4, BFinclusion = 0.136; interaction: F(1,31) = 6.2e-4, p=0.955, η²=1.0e-4, BFinclusion = 0.042).
evidence: This is a finding from the supplemental analysis of baseline pupil size.

claim: Pupil size during baseline was of a similar magnitude during both attention tasks and expectation conditions.
source: Thus, data suggest that pupil size, and thereby likely arousal, during baseline was of a similar magnitude during both attention tasks and expectation conditions, thereby rendering an explanation of the observed phasic differences in pupil size based on differences in baseline pupil size unlikely.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the supplemental analysis findings on baseline pupil size.
